name: Buddhist noon fast

card.summary: A daily or periodic fast from noon until the next sunrise, drawn from the Buddhist Eight Precepts, that some people adopt as a structured eating window for leanness and a sharper look.
card.aka: eight precepts fasting, sixth precept fast
card.note: A restricted eating window can be unsuitable for people with a history of disordered eating, diabetes or pregnancy; the religious practice permits liquids.

quick.overview:
The Buddhist noon fast comes from the sixth of the Eight Precepts, which asks lay followers to abstain from solid food after midday. Practitioners in Theravada traditions keep it on observance days, on retreat, or continuously in some monastic-style roles.

In fitness and looksmaxxing circles it is borrowed as a form of time-restricted eating: finish eating by noon, stay fasted until the next morning, with a leaner physique and clearer skin as the hoped-for payoff. The religious aim is concentration and reduced desire, and a cited commentary suggests the half-day fast is also said to improve fitness and reduce sleepiness.
quick.how: In the religious form, fluids are permitted and the fast is kept one day at a time on uposatha days or longer on retreats. Gym forum logs show a looser fitness variant of fasted mornings extended to around noon, sometimes with training in the fasted state.
quick.risks: Reduced eating windows can interact with training, appetite and mood, and one forum poster who tried intermittent fasting for years said it did not suit muscle building and fed binge eating. People with medical conditions are generally advised by clinicians to take advice before extended fasting.

lead: The Buddhist noon fast is the dietary rule within the Eight Precepts, a code lay Buddhists observe on uposatha days and at retreats. The sixth precept is to abstain from eating at the 'wrong time', meaning after midday, while liquids are allowed [1].

In a looksmaxxing and fitness context, the practice appears as a way to compress eating into the morning and early afternoon, aimed at staying lean or looking more defined. Scholars cited in the Wikipedia article argue the half-day fast reduces desire, improves fitness and strength and reduces sleepiness [1].

The religious practice has its own history: the precepts are described in the Pali Dhammika Sutta, were revived in late nineteenth-century Sri Lanka under Anagarika Dharmapala, and are kept continuously by some Thai mae chi nuns [1]. No published trial tests the noon rule itself as a physique or appearance protocol.

chain: Stop eating at noon until sunrise
Shorter daily eating window, fewer calories eaten late
Possible lower body fat and a leaner look
angle.text: Followers who adopt it for looks do so to keep calories and body fat down through a fixed daily cutoff. The effect on appearance is the adopter's expectation and depends on total intake.

paras: Lay followers usually keep the Eight Precepts for a single day, which is why they are sometimes called one-day precepts, and keeping them is thought to support meditation [1]. Some people keep them continuously, such as Thai mae chi nuns, and those preparing for ordination as monks also take them [1]. The practice is most associated with Theravada Buddhism in South and Southeast Asia [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness culture
paras: Lifters in training logs on T Nation describe fasting until noon, sometimes with morning walks, bodyweight work or coffee and supplements before the first meal [2][3]. One log describes a 30-hour fast from noon to the following evening after reading about routine fasting [4]. These are time-restricted eating variants of the same clock rather than the precept itself.
Opinions in the same forums differ. One poster who had used intermittent fasting since college wrote that it helped with studying but did not suit muscle building and contributed to binge eating [5].
No studies found on the noon precept as an appearance protocol. Research on time-restricted eating and intermittent fasting is a broader field.
